stem: What is the maximum number of benches the planner can include in the design?
stimulus: An urban planner is redesigning a pedestrian plaza with a budget of $\$12{,}000$ for trees and benches. Each tree costs $\$450$ to plant, and each bench costs $\$320$ to install. The city's green-space rule requires the plaza to have at least $12$ trees.
explanation: To leave as much money as possible for benches, you plant only the required minimum of $12$ trees, which costs $12(450) = 5{,}400$ dollars. That leaves $12{,}000 - 5{,}400 = 6{,}600$ dollars, so $320b \le 6{,}600$ and $b \le 20.625$. The number of benches must be a whole number, and this is a maximum, so you round down to $20$.

B.why: You rounded $20.625$ up to $21$. Twenty-one benches cost $6{,}720$ dollars, which goes over the $6{,}600$ dollars left for benches. For a maximum, you have to round down.

C.why: You added the $12$ trees to the $20$ benches and gave the total number of items. The question asks only for the number of benches.

D.why: You divided the whole budget by the bench price, $12{,}000 \div 320 = 37.5$, and ignored the rule that the plaza must have at least $12$ trees.

stem: What is the greatest altitude, in whole kilometers, at which the sensor will still read accurately?
stimulus: A meteorologist launches a weather balloon from a site where the air temperature is $18^{\circ}\text{C}$. On this day, the temperature falls by $6.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ for each kilometer of altitude gained. The balloon's humidity sensor reads accurately only when the air temperature is $-40^{\circ}\text{C}$ or warmer.
explanation: The temperature at altitude $h$ kilometers is $18 - 6.5h$, and it must satisfy $18 - 6.5h \ge -40$. Subtracting $18$ gives $-6.5h \ge -58$. When you divide by $-6.5$, the sign flips: $h \le 8.92$. For a maximum, you round down, so the answer is $8$ kilometers.

A.why: You took the temperature gap as $40 - 18 = 22$ degrees, which drops the negative sign on $-40$. The temperature actually has to fall $18 - (-40) = 58$ degrees.

C.why: You rounded $8.92$ up to $9$, or you forgot to flip the sign when you divided by $-6.5$. At $9$ km the temperature is $-40.5^{\circ}\text{C}$, which is too cold for the sensor.

D.why: $58$ is the total temperature drop the sensor can handle, in degrees. You still need to divide it by $6.5$ degrees per kilometer to get the altitude.

stem: What is the minimum number of parts for which Service A costs less than Service B?
stimulus: An orchestra's librarian is choosing between two services for renting the instrumental parts of a newly rediscovered symphony. Service A charges a flat fee of $\$60$ plus $\$4.50$ per part. Service B has no flat fee and charges $\$12$ per part.
explanation: Set up $60 + 4.5p < 12p$. Subtracting $4.5p$ from both sides gives $60 < 7.5p$, so $p > 8$. At exactly $8$ parts the two services both cost $\$96$, so Service A is not yet cheaper. The smallest whole number greater than $8$ is $9$.

A.why: You added the per-part rates, $60 \div (12 + 4.5) \approx 3.6$, and rounded up. You should subtract them, because Service A saves $12 - 4.5 = 7.5$ dollars on each part.

B.why: You divided the flat fee by Service B's rate, $60 \div 12 = 5$, and ignored the $\$4.50$ per part that Service A also charges.

C.why: You kept the boundary value. At $8$ parts both services cost $\$96$, so Service A is equal to Service B, not less. The strict inequality $p > 8$ rules out $8$.

stem: What is the minimum number of hours the technician must work in a week to earn at least $\$1{,}150$?
stimulus: A warehouse technician earns $\$22$ per hour for the first $40$ hours worked in a week. Every hour beyond $40$ in that week is paid at an overtime rate of $\$33$ per hour.
explanation: The first $40$ hours pay $40(22) = 880$ dollars, which leaves $1{,}150 - 880 = 270$ dollars to earn at the overtime rate. Solving $33x \ge 270$ gives $x \ge 8.18$, and because this is a minimum you round up to $9$ overtime hours. The total is $40 + 9 = 49$ hours, which pays $880 + 297 = 1{,}177$ dollars.

A.why: $9$ is the number of overtime hours only. The question asks for the total hours worked, so you still need to add the first $40$ hours.

B.why: You rounded $8.18$ down to $8$ overtime hours. Forty-eight hours pay only $880 + 264 = 1{,}144$ dollars, which is short of $\$1{,}150$. For a minimum, you round up.

D.why: You paid every hour at $\$22$, so $1{,}150 \div 22 \approx 52.3$ and you rounded up to $53$. This ignores the higher overtime rate for hours beyond $40$.

stem: What is the maximum number of whole hours the bird can fly nonstop while keeping its body mass at least $215$ grams?
stimulus: An ornithologist tracking a migrating godwit estimates that the bird begins a nonstop flight with a body mass of $320$ grams and burns off $7.5$ grams of mass for each hour it flies. To survive the journey, the bird's body mass must stay at least $215$ grams.
explanation: Set up $320 - 7.5h \ge 215$. Subtracting $320$ gives $-7.5h \ge -105$. Dividing by $-7.5$ flips the sign: $h \le 14$. "At least" means $\ge$, so the boundary is allowed. At $14$ hours the mass is exactly $215$ grams, so the maximum is $14$.

A.why: You treated "at least $215$ grams" as a strict inequality and threw out the boundary. At $14$ hours the mass is exactly $215$ grams, and that is allowed.

C.why: You probably didn't flip the sign when you divided by $-7.5$, which gives $h \ge 14$, and then picked the next whole number. At $15$ hours the mass is $207.5$ grams, which is below the limit.

D.why: You divided the starting mass by the hourly loss, $320 \div 7.5 \approx 42.7$. That is how long it would take the bird to lose all of its mass, and it ignores the $215$-gram floor.

stem: What is the minimum number of prints the printmaker must sell to guarantee a profit greater than $\$600$, no matter which price in the range each print sells for?
stimulus: A printmaker is producing an edition of linocut prints. Carving the block costs $\$420$ once, and each print costs $\$6$ in paper and ink. Depending on the venue, each print sells for anywhere from $\$35$ to $\$50$. Profit equals total sales minus total costs.
explanation: To guarantee the profit, you assume every print sells at the lowest price, $\$35$. The profit on $n$ prints is $35n - 6n - 420 = 29n - 420$, and you need $29n - 420 > 600$. That gives $29n > 1{,}020$, so $n > 35.17$. Rounding up gives $36$ prints, for a profit of $29(36) - 420 = 624$ dollars.

A.why: You used the highest price, $\$50$. That gives $44n > 1{,}020$ and $n > 23.2$. A guarantee has to hold even when every print sells for only $\$35$.

B.why: You left out the $\$6$ cost per print and solved $35n > 1{,}020$. Each print actually adds only $35 - 6 = 29$ dollars of profit.

C.why: You rounded $35.17$ down. Thirty-five prints give a profit of $29(35) - 420 = 595$ dollars, which is not greater than $\$600$. For a minimum, you round up.

stem: What is the maximum number of whole days the station can record before its data card must be replaced?
stimulus: A remote seismograph station stores its readings on a $32$-gigabyte (GB) data card. Calibration files that take up $2$ GB are loaded onto the card before recording begins, and the station then records $0.4$ GB of ground-motion data per day. To prevent write errors, at least $3$ GB of the card must remain free at all times.
explanation: The data used after $d$ days is $2 + 0.4d$, and it can be at most $32 - 3 = 29$ GB. So $2 + 0.4d \le 29$, which gives $0.4d \le 27$ and $d \le 67.5$. For a maximum, you round down to $67$ days.

A.why: $27$ is the number of gigabytes available for daily recordings. You still need to divide it by $0.4$ GB per day to get the number of days.

C.why: You rounded $67.5$ up. After $68$ days the card holds $29.2$ GB, which leaves less than the required $3$ GB free.

D.why: You divided $30$ GB by $0.4$. That subtracts the calibration files but forgets the $3$ GB that must stay free.

stem: Which inequality gives all values of $w$ for which Team B's dictionary has more entries than Team A's?
stimulus: Two teams of linguists are compiling dictionaries of an endangered language. Team A's dictionary currently has $2{,}600$ entries, and the team adds $50$ entries per week. Team B's dictionary currently has $1{,}850$ entries, and the team adds $75$ entries per week. Let $w$ be the number of weeks from now.
explanation: Set up $1{,}850 + 75w > 2{,}600 + 50w$. Subtracting $50w$ and $1{,}850$ from both sides gives $25w > 750$, so $w > 30$. At exactly $30$ weeks both dictionaries have $4{,}100$ entries, so $30$ itself is not included.

A.why: You divided the $750$-entry gap by Team B's rate alone, $750 \div 75 = 10$. This ignores that Team A keeps adding $50$ entries per week, so Team B closes the gap by only $25$ entries per week.

B.why: You reversed the direction of the inequality. Before week $30$, Team A is still ahead, so $w < 30$ gives the weeks when Team B has fewer entries.

D.why: You kept the boundary. At $w = 30$ the two dictionaries are tied at $4{,}100$ entries, and "more than" calls for a strict inequality.

stem: What is the maximum number of hours of fluent-speaker recordings the linguist can have transcribed?
stimulus: A linguist documenting a regional dialect has $\$1{,}400$ to spend on transcription. Recordings of fluent speakers cost $\$65$ per hour to transcribe, and recordings of learners cost $\$40$ per hour. The project requires that at least $8$ hours of learner recordings be transcribed, and only whole hours can be ordered.
explanation: To get the most fluent-speaker hours, spend as little as you can on learner recordings: the minimum of $8$ hours costs $40(8) = 320$ dollars. That leaves $1{,}400 - 320 = 1{,}080$ dollars, so $65f \le 1{,}080$ and $f \le 16.6\ldots$. The count has to be a whole number and can't go over the cap, so you round down to $16$ hours.

B.why: You solved $f \le 16.6\ldots$ correctly but rounded up. Seventeen hours would cost $65(17) + 320 = 1{,}425$ dollars, which is over budget. For a maximum, round down.

C.why: You divided the whole budget by $65$ ($1{,}400 / 65 \approx 21.5$) and ignored the requirement of at least $8$ learner hours. That requirement has to be paid for first.

D.why: You added the $8$ learner hours to the $16$ fluent hours and got the total hours transcribed. The question asks only for the fluent-speaker hours.

stem: What is the minimum whole number of hours of press time per month for which the membership plan costs less than the hourly plan?
stimulus: A printmaking studio offers two ways to rent its etching press. Under the hourly plan, an artist pays $\$15$ for each hour of press time. Under the membership plan, an artist pays a monthly fee of $\$240$ plus $\$3$ for each hour of press time.
explanation: Let $h$ be the number of hours. The membership plan costs less when $240 + 3h < 15h$. Subtract $3h$ from both sides to get $240 < 12h$, so $h > 20$. At exactly $20$ hours the two plans cost the same ($\$300$ each), so the membership plan is not yet cheaper. The smallest whole number greater than $20$ is $21$.

A.why: You added the hourly rates instead of subtracting them ($240 < 18h$, so $h > 13.3\ldots$, which rounds up to $14$). The $3h$ has to be subtracted from $15h$, not added to it.

B.why: You compared the $\$240$ fee with the hourly plan alone ($15h > 240$) and left out the membership plan's $\$3$ charge per hour.

C.why: At $20$ hours the plans cost the same, $\$300$ each. The question asks when the membership plan costs less, which is a strict inequality, so the boundary value doesn't count.

stem: What is the minimum number of additional full days of surveying that guarantees the team reaches its goal of 1,000 kilometers?
stimulus: A cartography team is mapping a long-distance hiking trail and must survey at least $1{,}000$ kilometers of it before its map can be published. The team has already surveyed $136$ kilometers. Depending on the terrain, the team surveys between $45$ and $60$ kilometers each full day.
explanation: The team still needs $1{,}000 - 136 = 864$ kilometers. To guarantee the goal, plan for the slowest possible day, $45$ kilometers: $45d \ge 864$ gives $d \ge 19.2$. A minimum count rounds up, so the answer is $20$ days.

A.why: You used the fastest rate, $60$ kilometers per day ($864 / 60 = 14.4$, which rounds up to $15$). That gives the fewest days the team might need, not the number that guarantees the goal. A guarantee has to hold even on the slowest days.

B.why: You solved $d \ge 19.2$ but rounded down. After $19$ slow days the team has covered only $855$ of the $864$ kilometers it needs. For a minimum, round up.

D.why: You divided the full $1{,}000$ kilometers by $45$ and forgot to subtract the $136$ kilometers already surveyed. You need the remaining distance, not the total.

stem: What is the greatest number of LED streetlights the city can install on the corridor?
stimulus: A city's budget for new streetlights on one corridor is at most $86,000. The project has a fixed permit fee of $5,000. Each LED streetlight costs $1,900 and each solar streetlight costs $2,700. The plan requires at least 12 solar streetlights.
explanation: Pay for the required items first so you can spend the rest on LED lights. The 12 solar lights cost $12(2700) = 32{,}400$ dollars. Together with the fee, that leaves $86{,}000 - 5{,}000 - 32{,}400 = 48{,}600$ dollars. Solve $1900x \le 48{,}600$ to get $x \le 25.58$. Because you are finding a maximum, round down to 25. Check: 25 LED lights bring the total to $84,900, which is within the budget, but 26 would bring it to $86,800, which is over.

A.why: You divided the remaining $48,600 by the solar price, $2,700, when you needed the LED price, $1,900.

C.why: You rounded 25.58 up. A count capped by a budget has to round down, and 26 lights would cost $86,800, which is more than $86,000.

D.why: You left out the requirement of at least 12 solar lights and spent everything after the fee on LED lights: $81{,}000 \div 1900 \approx 42.6$.

stem: What is the minimum number of contracts the employee must sign in a week for Offer B to pay more than Offer A?
stimulus: An employee is choosing between two job offers. Offer A pays a salary of $900 per week. Offer B pays $420 per week plus $40 for each contract signed, minus a weekly equipment fee of $80.
explanation: Offer B's weekly pay is $420 + 40c - 80 = 340 + 40c$. Set up $340 + 40c > 900$, which gives $40c > 560$ and $c > 14$. The inequality is strict, so 14 contracts only makes Offer B equal to Offer A. The smallest whole number greater than 14 is 15.

A.why: You left out the $80 equipment fee. Solving $420 + 40c > 900$ gives $c > 12$, and the next whole number is 13.

B.why: You kept the boundary value. At 14 contracts both offers pay exactly $900, and the question asks for Offer B to pay more.

D.why: You dropped Offer B's base pay and fee and solved $40c > 900$, which gives 22.5, and then rounded up to 23.

stem: What is the maximum number of full excavation units the team can complete this season?
stimulus: An archaeology team has at most 160 hours of labor for a field season. Setting up the site takes 18 hours. The team must dig at least 4 test pits, which take 2.5 hours each. Each full excavation unit takes 7 hours.
explanation: Pay for setup and the required test pits first: $18 + 4(2.5) = 28$ hours. That leaves $160 - 28 = 132$ hours. Solve $7u \le 132$ to get $u \le 18.86$. For a maximum, round down to 18. Check: 18 units bring the total to 154 hours, but 19 would bring it to 161 hours, which is over the limit.

B.why: You rounded 18.86 up. The team doesn't have enough hours to finish a 19th unit, because that would need 161 hours.

C.why: You left out the 4 required test pits and divided $160 - 18 = 142$ hours by 7, which is about 20.3.

D.why: You left out the 18 setup hours and divided $160 - 10 = 150$ hours by 7, which is about 21.4.

stem: What is the minimum number of additional sessions the linguist must record?
stimulus: A linguist documenting a regional dialect needs at least 620 minutes of usable audio. She already has 95 usable minutes. Each new recording session lasts 50 minutes, but 8 minutes of every session are unusable because of background noise.
explanation: Each session gives $50 - 8 = 42$ usable minutes. Set up $95 + 42s \ge 620$, which gives $42s \ge 525$ and $s \ge 12.5$. Because you are finding a minimum, round up to 13. Twelve sessions would bring her to only 599 minutes.

A.why: You used the full 50 minutes per session in place of the 42 usable minutes, so you got $525 \div 50 = 10.5$ and rounded up to 11.

B.why: You rounded 12.5 down. For a minimum you have to round up, and 12 sessions bring her to only 599 minutes.

D.why: You left out the 95 minutes she already has and solved $42s \ge 620$, which gives about 14.8, and then rounded up to 15.

stem: What is the greatest number of crackers the patient can eat that day and be certain of staying within the limit?
stimulus: A dietitian limits a patient to at most 2,300 milligrams (mg) of sodium per day. The patient's planned meals for one day contain 1,610 mg of sodium. The crackers the patient eats contain between 45 mg and 60 mg of sodium each, depending on the brand.
explanation: The meals leave $2300 - 1610 = 690$ mg. To be certain of staying within the limit, use the worst case of 60 mg per cracker. Solve $60c \le 690$ to get $c \le 11.5$. For a maximum, round down to 11.

B.why: You rounded 11.5 up. Twelve crackers at 60 mg each add 720 mg, which goes over the 690 mg left.

C.why: You used the lowest sodium value, 45 mg, so you got $690 \div 45 \approx 15.3$. With a higher-sodium brand, 15 crackers would go over the limit.

D.why: You left out the 1,610 mg already in the meals and divided the whole 2,300 mg by 60, which is about 38.3.
